description: Hinomaru Signal (Lima). Construimos una herramienta para elegir dónde y cuándo aterrizar en el polo sur lunar: vista desde el lander con el horizonte real, el Sol y la Tierra, cuenta regresiva al atardecer y comparación de sitios y fechas en segundos. Estephano hace toda la programación y el diseño UX/UI (React, PostGIS, 3D, datos de JPL Horizons y LOLA). Buscamos 1 o 2 personas para video, storytelling y pitch, o con base en astronomía. ¡Únete!
summary:
Horizon Signal is a web application for comparing landing sites and dates at the Moon's south pole. For a chosen site, date and length of stay, it draws the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, shows how long each one stays in view, and gives a GO, REVIEW or NO GO verdict against the mission's own requirements: Sun and Earth in view at landing, a night no longer than the battery lasts, and a minimum share of Earth contact. When a plan fails, for example because the launch date slipped, the tool proposes how to comply: another date, another zone, or taller equipment. Up to six scenarios can be compared side by side.

It addresses the challenge by turning JPL Horizons ephemerides and LOLA terrain data into an answer a non-specialist can read quickly, with the exact figures available for engineers. A 3D Moon with 62 landing sites and a voice guide also make it useful for teaching.

It matters because at the pole a small change of site or date changes power and communication, and mission schedules rarely hold.
details:
Horizon SignAl

A lunar South Pole mission planner featuring an AI assistant named EVA, who guides users through every screen. It allows users to select where and when to land based on the positions of the Sun and Earth, track the mission campaign in its logbook, plan astronaut surface walks, and simulate the landing descent. Each mission is linked to the planner, where the engine calculates the positions of the Sun and Earth using JPL Horizons ephemerides.

1. Dawn Breaks at the South Pole

The team can see at a glance which mission is ready, which is awaiting approval, and what has changed, without having to cross-reference spreadsheets or specialized tools. Every decision is recorded in the logbook with its date, mission, and type (plan, simulation, approval), ensuring a fully traceable history. Engineering, science, and flight operations all work with the same data.

2. Planner Views

- Allows for quick replanning when a launch is delayed: simply adjust the date and instantly see whether the landing site remains viable.

- Transforms data that would normally require expertise in ephemerides and lunar cartography into a clear, visual decision.

3. The Mission Campaign LogbookA 3D lunar globe featuring real NASA terrain data (LRO LOLA), bringing together 62 landing sites, ranging from Apollo, Luna, Chang'e, and SLIM to South Pole candidate sites. Each site includes its source and is classified by type: crewed, robotic, sample return, rover, polar candidate, or impact.

The real Sun and Earth: Choose a date between 2026 and 2030, and the globe is illuminated by the actual Sun position at that time (based on JPL ephemerides). You can animate time by hours or days to see how lighting and shadows change, and determine from which sites the Sun and Earth are visible above the horizon.

4. Simulated Lunar Landing

An Apollo-style descent to the selected landing site, featuring real-time altitude, velocity, thrust, and fuel levels, along with a descent map and altitude profile leading up to touchdown. The guidance system is validated against the Apollo 11 flight plan and even includes Armstrong's famous 1202 alarm.

5. Mission Simulation

After touchdown, the view switches to the helmet display: oxygen, CO₂, water, battery, and heart rate, with real-time alerts indicating whether the terrain blocks visibility of the Sun or Earth. EVA, the AI assistant, appears as a hologram, explains the spacesuit systems, warns when any parameter enters the red zone, and guides the scientific route stop by stop.

4. Technology

Frontend (apps/web)

- React 19, React DOM, React Router 8, TypeScript 5.8, Vite 7

- 3D: three.js 0.187, React Three Fiber, drei, Draco decoder

- Animation and scrolling: GSAP, Lenis

- EVA assistant: react-markdown and remark-gfm; in-browser voice detection with Silero VAD (@ricky0123/vad-web) on ONNX Runtime Web

- Fonts: Archivo and IBM Plex Mono (Fontsource); Jost, Inter and Space Grotesk (Google Fonts)

Backend (apps/api)

- Node.js 22 with Hono and @hono/node-server, postgres.js, undici

- @anthropic-ai/sdk: option to use Claude in the cloud instead of the team's own servers

- ElevenLabs: optional cloud voice, enabled with API keys

Planner (prototipos/lunar-map)

- Static HTML, CSS and JavaScript; engine.js is the engine ported to JavaScript

Database (db/)

- PostgreSQL 17 with PostGIS 3.5 (image postgis/postgis:17-3.5)

- Data loading (ETL) in Python 3.12 with psycopg, NumPy and Pillow

AI and voice (voz/, on the team's own GPU servers)

- Ollama with Qwen: qwen3.6:27b for answers and qwen3:8b to classify interruptions

- Speech synthesis: Kokoro-82M with misaki, spaCy en_core_web_sm and espeak-ng; also qwen-tts

- Speech recognition: faster-whisper large-v3-turbo (CUDA/cuBLAS)

- Server: FastAPI and uvicorn

- Custom RAG (apps/api/src/assistant/rag.ts)

Engine and earlier prototype (luna-recursos)

- Bun for the data scripts and tests, and oxlint

- Apache 2.0 license

Infrastructure

- Docker (node:22-alpine, python:3.12-slim) and Docker Compose

- GitHub Actions (CI and deployment)

- nginx with two copies of the app, so deployments don't take the site down

- Playwright and concurrently

Continuity proposal:

As a collaboration proposal, we aim to continue our research with the University of Padua (Italy), because it studies satellite constellations in halo orbits around the Lagrange points L1 and L2. Its proposed configuration of three satellites around L2 and one around L1 guarantees continuous communication coverage at the lunar south pole, solving the problem of the lack of communication between Earth and the NASA team.
